"Mumma, look!"
Afreen turned from the stove. Lalit stood holding the kitchen scissors. Half his fringe was gone; the rest stuck out sideways.
"Lalit! Why?"
"I wanted it short like cousin Dev's. I thought it would be easy." His lip wobbled. "It went crooked."
Afreen took the scissors gently. "Scissors near your eyes can hurt you."
"Can you make it go back?"
"No, beta. It will grow. Tomorrow the barber will make it even."
Lalit looked in the steel pot lid and cried. "I look silly."
Afreen hugged him. "Next time, ask first."

qa.a: Afreen is shocked at first, worried about the scissors near his eyes, then gentle, hugging him and planning a barber visit.

Preschool note to parents: Thomas, Tuesday

At craft time today, while I was helping another child, Thomas used the round-tipped scissors to cut his own fringe. "I wanted it spiky like my cousin's," he told me. It is now very uneven. When he saw the mirror in the bathroom he became upset and hid his face in his hands. I sat with him, told him hair grows back, and we talked about asking a grown-up first. Please don't scold him; he feels bad enough. Bidisha, our assistant, will keep scissors on the teacher's table during free play now.

qa.q: Where did Thomas see his fringe after cutting it?
qa.a: In the mirror in the bathroom.

qa.q: How did Thomas feel when he saw his fringe?
qa.a: He was very upset and ashamed; he hid his face in his hands.

qa.q: How could Thomas's parents support him at home?
qa.a: Stay calm, reassure him his hair will grow, and gently remind him to ask a grown-up before trying something new.

qa.q: How might Bidisha see the change to where scissors are kept?
qa.a: Bidisha likely sees it as a small, sensible step to keep the children safe during free play.
